cells.tense: You're here in it, and you're the one tending what lives and what gets built — both at once, and it's holding.
cells.ask: Tell one person who's watched you do this that a stretch of it is done — out loud, once — and let that be the end of the stretch, so the care that follows starts from a spent account rather than a guarded one.
cells.core:
You decide what gets fed and what gets built, and you do it with both hands. Two demands that usually pull against each other, and you keep them in the same motion — the caring and the making. People around you feel it; things under your care keep coming up.

The one move that hasn't happened is someone saying it, or you letting it be said. The care works whether or not it gets counted. But work that nobody marks tends to just keep going, and rest slides to whatever comes after. Letting someone see what you've been carrying, and letting that be enough for now, is what frees the next growing thing to start without the last one still asking for you.

cells.tense: You're already living a few steps ahead of where any of this actually is, bracing for what it'll take to keep it standing.
cells.ask: Leave one thing you're carrying at the stage it's at for a full day — no advancing it, no propping it up — and notice what the day itself does with it.
cells.core:
You're out ahead of it. The whole future already belongs to you in advance — next month's version, next year's, every way this could go — so nothing can catch you out. From out there, what's actually here today gets less of you, and the growing things feel the grip even through the care.

Care that doesn't exhaust is still on the table. It starts by putting the bracing down. One thing stays where it is for a day. The timing you're trying to secure hasn't arrived and won't be secured by holding it. Letting a thing develop without your hand on it every hour is the rest you've been trying to earn by staying ahead of everything.

cells.tense: For a while now you've been near this without picking it up, and the way forward sits behind where you're standing.
cells.ask: Put one thing you're tending in front of the person it's actually for and ask them one real question about it — even if you're not sure it's the right question.
cells.core:
When this part is working, you move through what's unclear the way you move through a room you know in the dark — one step at a time, trusting the next inch over the whole picture. Nothing forces it. The path shows itself and you take it.

Right now you've stopped taking it. The part of you that used to move things forward is quiet, and you stand close to the work without picking it up. Somewhere near it is where you waited for the rest of the road to show up before moving, and the waiting became the place you live. One real question to one real person about something you're tending pulls the current back through. Curious about an outcome you can't control is how this returns — not sure of it.

cells.tense: You're already cultivating this and you're calling it something that happened on its own.
cells.ask: Take one piece of what's around you — the timing, the resources, the way it came together — and say to someone that you're the one who shaped it, in your own words, once.
cells.core:
You tell the story as if the work did itself — the timing, the resources, the way it all came together. In how you decide what to keep and what to let go, you've been the one doing it the whole time.

Not owning it keeps it small, and it keeps you off the hook for what it becomes — which is also what keeps you from what it could be if you named what you're doing to it. Saying it's yours, once, in plain words, is not a claim on the outcome. It's a claim on the part that's actually been yours.
